entry.evidence: little is currently known about how this influences the net suspended sediment flux

sequences.source_document: Published paper (PDF), with publisher XML text for abstract and captions

steps.action: Pose the question of how turbulence-driven aggregation and disaggregation of flocs affects the net, size-resolved suspended sediment flux in a tidal sea.
steps.quote: little is currently known about how this influences the net suspended sediment flux

steps.action: Choose a tidal strait, where flux is confined to one axis, with observing sites on either side of a central region of strong turbulence (the Swellies), and plan to compare the observations with a simple model.
steps.quote: [...] , in which the flux is confined to be in one of two directions, makes a good site for observing

steps.action: Use Harker's (1997) along-strait surface SPM transects to show that suspended load is not elevated at the fast-flowing Swellies.
steps.quote: There is a deal of scatter in these points but little evidence of high suspended load corresponding to the fast currents in the Swellies.

steps.action: Draw on the authors' earlier Plas Newydd LISST study (Braithwaite et al. 2012), which separated local and advective components of particle size change and inferred the sense of the longitudinal size gradient.
steps.quote: the sense of the longitudinal particle size gradient was inferred from the correlation between measured particle size at the site and the tidal displacement

steps.action: Survey four cross-strait stations at Menai Bridge over one tidal cycle on 17 November 2015, measuring ADCP velocity profiles, LISST 100X size-resolved volume profiles and surface gravimetric SPM samples, and integrate volume concentration times velocity over depth, width and time to get the flux per size class.
steps.quote: observations were made of particle concentration and current velocity in a section of the strait at Menai Bridge

steps.action: Calibrate LISST total volume against gravimetric mass by linear regression (M = 1.34 + 0.213 V, R2 = 0.54), giving an average apparent particle density of 213 kg m-3 under a constant-density assumption.
steps.quote: Gravimetrically determined SPM concentrations were used to calibrate the total volume of particles measured by the LISST into an equivalent mass.

steps.action: Following a reviewer's suggestion to use fractal floc density for size-resolved mass fluxes, test the fractal method on an earlier Menai Strait data set; it agrees with measured mass but is not applied here because mass concentrations are missing at some stations.
steps.quote: test the method on an earlier data set from the Menai Strait and found that the fractal theory gave excellent agreement to measured mass

steps.action: Re-analyse the September 2008 bed-frame data set from Plas Newydd, south-west of the Swellies (ADCP, LISST-100C about 0.5 m above the bed, 9 tidal cycles), computing particle flux from near-bed volume concentration times depth-mean speed and water depth.
steps.quote: we have re-analysed a data set collected in September 2008 at Plas Newydd, to the south-west of the Swellies

steps.action: At Menai Bridge, establish that D50 falls at peak currents, falls more on the flood (flow from the Swellies), that the column is nearly vertically homogeneous, and that the tidal-mean flux is size-dependent: small particles flow north-east away from the Swellies and large ones flow south-west towards them.
steps.quote: The smallest particles (up to about 50 μm) are being transported towards the north-east, that is away from the Swellies

steps.action: Check the pattern with the independent 2008 Plas Newydd data from the other side of the Swellies (last three storm-free cycles). They show the mirror image: smallest particles when flow comes from the Swellies, large particles (>125 μm) moving towards the Swellies and small ones away, with residual current removed; other cycles show a similar flux pattern.
steps.quote: The variation in particle size at Plas Newydd is a mirror image of that seen at Menai Bridge.

steps.action: Set the local-process explanation (resuspension of large particles carried with the current) against the proposal that turbulence in the Swellies breaks up flocs, which are advected outwards, re-form, and return as large particles.
steps.quote: We propose that a more likely explanation is that the strong turbulence in the Swellies tears up flocs.

steps.action: Reject local processes alone, by argument: locally resuspended large particles would move with the current and give no convergence towards the centre from both sides.
steps.quote: These observations cannot be explained by local processes alone.

steps.action: Build a diagnostic 1-D model of an idealised 25 km strait: the Winterwerp (1998) floc equation with the Braithwaite et al. (2012) constants, recast as two size classes (25 and 125 μm) with advection, a symmetric sinusoidal tide whose amplitude ramps to 1.5 m/s in the centre, no settling or residual flow, solved by forward time-stepping with upwind differencing.
steps.quote: Our aim here is to try a diagnostic model of a tidal strait with a region of fast tidal streams in the central portion

steps.action: Compare model output with the observations. Modelled size at the Menai Bridge and Plas Newydd analogue points reaches its minimum when flow comes from the centre, matching the observations, though the size ranges differ. Modelled tidal-mean fluxes carry large particles towards the centre and small ones away, with flux maxima about 4 km either side. Term analysis puts advection at about 10% of aggregation and break-up.
steps.quote: These patterns are similar to those seen in the observations.

steps.action: Retain the claim of a tidal-mean net transport of large particles from the ends towards the centre and of small particles outwards, consistent across two campaigns that differ in method, season and site.
steps.quote: Despite the differences in the way the data was collected, there are striking similarities between the temporal patterns of particle size

steps.action: Estimate the magnitude of the peak transport: 10-60 m3 of particles per tide, about 2000-13,000 kg per tide using the 213 kg m-3 apparent density, and a flux per unit area of 1-6.5 × 10-5 kg m-2 s-1.
steps.quote: the mass transport peaks at between about 2000 and 13,000 kg per tide

steps.action: Check the model's omitted settling and resuspension against the vertical profiles (no resuspension at fast currents) and a settling-speed scale estimate (about 60 cm fall during a 10-min slack).
steps.quote: The vertical profiles shown in Fig. 6 show no evidence of resuspension at times of fast currents.

steps.action: Recast the tidal wake mechanism as the effective diffusion of the Bowers et al. (2005) ITM model, deriving K = u²T (about 450 m2 s-1 for u = 0.5 m/s and T = 30 min), a value judged reasonable against Simpson and Sharples (2012).
steps.quote: the product uL is therefore equivalent to a diffusion coefficient

steps.action: Compare with Harker's SPM data to conclude that the Swellies is not an isolated turbidity maximum, although its size-dependent fluxes are analogous to those in an ITM.
steps.quote: The Swellies region of the Menai Strait is not an isolated turbidity maximum as far as we can tell.

steps.action: Pose follow-on questions on the relevance of tidal diffusion to ITM maintenance and on the timescales of floc formation and break-up, proposing the strait as a natural laboratory.
steps.quote: would make an excellent natural laboratory in which to study these processes

tree.answer: Floc size depends on flow direction relative to the Swellies, and the tidal-mean flux direction depends on particle size
Size and velocity observed directly; flux computed, mass from calibration
Measure size-resolved transport and explain it with a simple model
Local resuspension versus central floc break-up plus tidal advection
Local processes give no convergence; the break-up model predicts large particles moving in and small ones out on both sides
Conditions found: natural tidal cycles at two sites in two campaigns

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Tides repeat; three coherent cycles at Plas Newydd, one at Menai Bridge
Mirror-image pattern on the opposite side in an independent data set; the model reproduces it qualitatively
Central break-up explanation kept as the best explanation
A referee suggested fractal mass fluxes; the method was tested on earlier data but not applied

end.claim: Strong turbulence in the Swellies breaks up flocs, which the tide carries outwards, so that over a tidal cycle there is a net flux of larger particles into the Swellies and of small particles out.

decisive_move.sentence: The re-analysed Plas Newydd data, showing the mirror image of the Menai Bridge pattern on the opposite side of the Swellies, are what make the convergence argument against local processes possible.

gates.evidence: Action: the 2015 survey was designed to measure size-resolved fluxes near a strong-turbulence region, and the introduction states the prior ITM finding of large flocs in and small out (p. 2). No hypothesis is stated as directing it, and the 2008 data came from an earlier study. Claim: the second site could have failed to show the mirror pattern, and the model was built after the observations to 'test this interpretation' (p. 5). The model is diagnostic and idealised, and its agreement is qualitative, with numerical size ranges that differ (p. 7). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Fractal model of floc structure for size-dependent density (Kranenburg 1994)
LISST laser in-situ scattering particle sizer
Forward time-stepping with upwind differencing for advection

novelty_claims.quote: there has been little previous work on the transport of different size particles responding to tidal aggregation and disaggregation in a shelf sea environment
An insight provided by the model is that there are points either side of the centre where the fluxes are greatest.

limits: Locations: the XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite PDF pages. No review file was supplied; the only review trace is the published acknowledgement that referee Friedrichs suggested fractal mass fluxes, so no review sequence is coded. Order of work: inference only; 'To test this interpretation' (p. 5) suggests the model was built after the observations. Evidence base: Menai Bridge rests on one tidal cycle disturbed by a storm, and only the last three of nine Plas Newydd cycles are shown. The two campaigns differ in season, sampling depth (near-bed versus full column) and platform. No uncertainties are given for the size-resolved fluxes. Mass conversion assumes constant floc density, which the authors note is often violated. The rival 'local processes' is rejected by argument, not by a quantitative test. The model omits settling, residual flow, tidal asymmetry and realistic bathymetry, and differs from the observations in numerical size range. Sub-claims: the transport magnitude (2000-13,000 kg per tide) is an order-of-magnitude estimate without stated uncertainty (estimate_with_resolution, weakly); K = u²T at about 450 m2/s is a scale argument (best_explanation); relevance to ITM maintenance is a suggestion (none); 'Swellies is not an ITM' rests on cited Harker data with no measurements in the Swellies (best_explanation).

disagreements.target: Bowers et al. (2005) ITM model with diffusion of small particles out and large particles in
disagreements.support: The observed and modelled tidal transport of size classes is recast as an effective diffusion K = u²T, implying that the 'diffusion' of the ITM model is produced by the tide itself.
disagreements.quote: The observations of this paper can be interpreted in a way which gives some insight into this ‘diffusion’ process.
